articles.title: From Jobs to Skills: Rethinking Vietnam’s FDI success
articles.full_text:
Despite its rapid industrialization, the country’s economy is not creating enough jobs that make productive use of advanced skills.
People riding motorbikes in Hanoi, Vietnam, Jan. 3, 2018.
Vietnam attracted $34.65 billion in registered foreign direct investment (FDI) in the first half of 2026, 61 percent more than the same period in 2025. At the same time, realized FDI reached $13.03 billion, its highest first-half level in five years. Observers including Harvard’s Growth Lab have also pointed to Vietnam’s increasingly diverse and sophisticated export base as a source of strong long-run growth prospects. By conventional measures, the country’s development model is working.
Despite this, another important labor-market signal has been moving in the opposite direction. Since the late 2000s, the wage premium earned by staying in school has been falling, with particularly marked falls for university graduates. This does not necessarily mean that education has become less valuable in itself. It may instead mean that the economy is not creating enough jobs that make productive use of advanced skills.
Whatever the reality, it has important implications for the Vietnamese government’s ambition of reaching high-income status by 2045. The gains from moving workers out of agriculture and into factories and services cannot continue indefinitely; future growth requires sustained productivity growth rather than labor reallocation alone. So far, Vietnam’s FDI model has succeeded on employment quantity but underperformed on occupational upgrading.
Drawing on 13 years of nationally representative Labor Force Survey data, a recent study that we conducted found that for every 100 jobs created in foreign-invested firms, an additional 100 jobs emerge in the same district – a local employment multiplier of roughly one to one. This is a large spillover, and a compelling reason why FDI has become such a central part of Vietnam’s growth story.
Foreign firms accounted for around one-tenth of total employment in 2023, up from almost nothing before 2000. Factory jobs raise household incomes and local spending, creating employment in other businesses.
The composition of these additional jobs, however, presents a more sobering picture. Of every 100 additional non-FDI jobs associated with foreign investment, roughly two-thirds are in services and only one-third in manufacturing. Most are generated by small, often informal household enterprises: i.e., the restaurants, repair shops, and retail stalls that spring up around industrial zones to serve factory workers.
Looking at the occupations themselves reveals the same pattern. For every 100 FDI jobs, only about 13 to 15 additional high-skilled cognitive jobs emerge, compared with 41 to 45 blue-collar production jobs and 27 to 31 clerical or service positions. The educational profile of jobs created elsewhere in the local economy largely mirrors Vietnam’s existing workforce, in which lower-secondary education predominates. Put simply, Vietnam’s FDI-led expansion has overwhelmingly been a jobs boom built on basic schooling rather than a skills boom. That helps explain why the country’s impressive educational progress has yet to translate into equally strong economic returns to education.
Vietnam has continued to invest in education. By 2023, workers with tertiary qualifications accounted for about 18 percent of total employment. Yet the economy has struggled to put those skills to productive use. Manufacturing employed 25.4 percent of the workforce but only 16.5 percent of tertiary-educated workers. Just 11.5 percent of manufacturing workers held a tertiary qualification, below the economy-wide average.
FDI-intensive provinces generally offer higher nominal wages. But the additional wage premium is not larger for better-educated workers. Moreover, part of the apparent wage advantage may simply compensate for higher housing and service costs in fast-growing industrial locations. FDI can therefore raise wages without necessarily strengthening the financial reward for remaining in education.
This changes the choices facing households. When a reasonably paid factory job is available after lower-secondary school, continuing in education becomes more costly, especially for poorer households that cannot easily forgo an immediate income. Grade 9 completion rate is now more than 90 percent, but Grade 12 completion remains below 60 percent. Simply expanding university places will not solve this demand-side problem. Unless the economy creates more jobs that reward advanced skills, Vietnam risks experiencing a growing graduate mismatch, in which educated workers are pushed into relatively low-productivity services, progression through upper-secondary education slows, and the country continues to lose talent abroad.
The policy question, therefore, is how to make capital, technology, and skills complementary. This is not an argument against foreign investment. FDI has been central to Vietnam’s structural transformation, export growth, and employment creation, and will continue to be so.
But it does suggest that Vietnam should broaden its definition of high-quality investment. Registered capital, exports, and headline job numbers should be assessed alongside occupational upgrading, wage progression, firm-based training, technical and managerial employment, engineering and research functions, and durable local-supplier development. Policymakers should distinguish a local spending multiplier from a productive capability spillover. A new restaurant or transport job is valuable, but it is not equivalent to a new engineering team, supplier certification, or transfer of production know-how.
Introducing local-content or skills quotas would be risky, and flexible investors may simply respond by locating elsewhere. More promising are incentive-compatible measures that lower the cost of undertaking sophisticated activities in Vietnam. These include reliable infrastructure, industry-linked training, applied research support, innovation services, and predictable regulation. Far from abandoning labor-intensive FDI, Vietnam’s objective should be to ensure that investment shifts towards more complex tasks and creates ladders within and beyond the factory.
Another part of the solution lies in Vietnam’s domestic economy. Resolution 68, issued by the Politburo of the Communist Party of Vietnam in May 2025, identifies the private sector as the most important driving force of future growth. That is a step in the right direction, but its success will be judged on whether a wide range of domestic firms can acquire technology, discover profitable niches, and scale up their operations.
Domestic firms are indispensable to Vietnam’s economic future because productive capabilities become embedded in an economy only when local businesses can learn from foreign investors, supply them, compete with them and develop innovations of their own. Better access to finance, easier formalization, and fairer competition would allow young and medium-sized firms to experiment, invest, and hire skilled workers. Export-promotion and network-building institutions can help them find buyers, enter global value chains, and learn from international partners.
Education policy must also connect more directly to labor demand. Public-private training partnerships, apprenticeships, and jointly designed curricula can improve matching, but they should be evaluated by whether graduates move into jobs that use and deepen their skills.
Place matters as well. Industrial and urban policy should combine reliable infrastructure with universities, vocational colleges, applied research centers, transport, housing, and public amenities. Such clusters could attract more sophisticated activities and the mobile skilled workers they require.
Vietnam does not need to choose between foreign investment and domestic enterprises. It needs domestic firms capable of learning from, supplying and eventually competing alongside foreign investors; and foreign investors whose success increasingly depends on Vietnamese skills and capabilities.
The fact that FDI has had a local jobs multiplier effect is worth celebrating, but is not evidence of technological or human-capital upgrading. Vietnam’s earlier growth model mobilized labor from agriculture into manufacturing; the model of the future must reward learning, innovation, and productivity.

articles.title: Thailand Pledges to Work Towards Myanmar’s Full Reintegration With ASEAN
articles.full_text:
The pledge came as Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul hosted the country’s military-appointed president, Min Aung Hlaing, in Bangkok.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing walk past a guard of honor in Bangkok, Thailand, Aug. 6, 2026.
Thailand has affirmed its intention to bring Myanmar back into the ASEAN fold, following a meeting between Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and the country’s military-appointed president, Min Aung Hlaing, in Bangkok yesterday.
The summit was the highlight of the former general’s two-day visit to Thailand, his first official visit to the country since he led a military coup in 2021.
After arriving in Bangkok, Min Aung Hlaing was given a red-carpet welcome by Anutin, who then hosted him for talks at Government House in Bangkok. During the visit, Min Aung Hlaing also attended an official dinner, met the leaders of both houses of the Thai parliament, and spoke at a Thai-Myanmar business forum in the Thai capital, before departing today.
In a joint statement issued late yesterday, Thailand “reaffirmed its commitment to supporting and continuing to work closely with Myanmar for Myanmar’s full and equal participation in ASEAN mechanisms and processes.” Myanmar in turn “expressed its appreciation for Thailand’s constructive role in facilitating the normalization of its relations with ASEAN.”
In the statement, the two countries said they agreed to “further deepen dialogue at all levels,” in the areas of security, trade, and environmental protection. They also expressed their “joint commitment to achieve a peaceful and stable Thailand–Myanmar border.”
The visit saw the signing of three bilateral deals between the two nations. As per Nikkei Asia, these included an agreement on Burmese migrant labor in Thailand and another setting up a joint working group to address river pollution from rare-earth mining. The two leaders also reportedly discussed ways to boost cross-border trade, including the resumption of trade over the Second Friendship Bridge connecting the Thai town of Mae Sot with Myawaddy in eastern Myanmar.
Thailand’s invitation to Min Aung Hlaing reflects its determination to bring Myanmar back in from the cold, after five years in which the country has been barred from ASEAN’s summits. The reason for its exclusion is its refusal to implement the Five-Point Consensus, ASEAN’s plan for managing Myanmar’s ramifying conflicts. Agreed in April 2021, the Consensus called for an immediate cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and political dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
For several years, Thailand has advocated engagement with the military junta in Naypyidaw, arguing that this is necessary to address issues like border security and transnational crime. This effort has redoubled since Min Aung Hlaing’s new “civilian” government took office in April. Since then, Bangkok has advocated a policy of “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar, and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow has also called for Myanmar to return to the “ASEAN family.”
During his meeting with Anutin, Min Aung Hlaing pressed the case for normalization, asserting that his government, which took office in April, was focused on ending the interlocking conflicts that have raged since the 2021 coup.
“Myanmar has now reestablished itself on the path to democracy and is moving toward a better future,” he said. “As the new government, we have now begun working on national stability, peace, and national reconciliation.” Speaking at the Thai-Myanmar business forum, he told attendees that they could “invest with confidence” in Myanmar’s energy, agriculture, manufacturing, and healthcare sectors.
Thailand’s invitation to Min Aung Hlaing has been roundly criticized by human rights advocates, who claim that it is undermining ASEAN’s efforts and helping the Myanmar military launder its international reputation. They have also pointed out that there has been no reduction in the frequency or severity of the military’s attacks on civilian populations since Min Aung Hlaing’s new government took office.
“Prime Minister Anutin should be ashamed to host Min Aung Hlaing, a murderous Myanmar military officer with the blood of countless Burmese on his hands,” Phil Robertson, the director of the rights group Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates, said in a statement. “When is Thailand going to wake up and realize that Min Aung Hlaing and his military compatriots are the core problem in Myanmar – and never will be part of the solution?” Aung Zaw, the editor of The Irrawaddy, wrote this week that Thailand “should not lend legitimacy to the thuggish regime in Naypyidaw.”
However, at a press conference yesterday after the summit between Anutin and Min Aung Hlaing, Sihasak rejected accusations that the kingdom is according legitimacy to Min Aung Hlaing.
“It’s not about legitimacy, it’s about reality,” he said, according to the Straits Times. “We have problems that we face along the border, and at the same time, we have to be proactive in terms of helping Myanmar on the path of peace, stability.” He added, “And the best way to achieve that is to have talks with those who are in the position of power.”
In any event, junta propaganda accounts on X gloated about the welcome accorded Min Aung Hlaing. “In accordance with international diplomatic customs, at the airport, there was a red carpet reception and a salute from the honor guard,” one account wrote. This, along with the official welcome ceremony outside Government House, “strongly reinforces legitimacy and paves a smooth path for bilateral cooperation,” it added.
How all this will play into ASEAN’s efforts to resolve Myanmar’s conflict remains unclear. The 11-nation bloc continues to demand action to implement the Five-Point Consensus (as does Thailand), and ASEAN’s special envoy for Myanmar, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said last month that Myanmar’s full reintegration with ASEAN was still “far off.”
At the same time, Min Aung Hlaing’s government has moved from implicit to full-throated rejection of the Five-Point Consensus. In a speech on July 31 marking his administration’s 100th day in office, Min Aung Hlaing declared that the Consensus was “not the consensus of all ASEAN member states” and that it was merely an annex attached to a statement by ASEAN’s then-chair, Brunei. This came after the military-dominated Union Parliament passed a resolution rejecting the Five-Point Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, stating that it “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.”
The contending positions – ASEAN’s adherence to the Five-Point Consensus and Naypyidaw’s rejection of the same – would seem to be a recipe for deadlock. It remains to be seen whether Thailand’s policy of “calibrated engagement” will offer an incentive for Myanmar to begin even token implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, or merely provide the junta with a path back to regional respectability.

articles.title: How the World Learned to Live with the Exclusion of Afghan Women
articles.full_text:
The world has to do more than admire Afghan women’s resilience. It must stand with them by taking concrete actions.
Five years ago, when the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, the world watched in shock as images emerged of desperate Afghans trying to escape a country whose future had suddenly changed. For Afghan women and girls, however, the fall of Afghanistan was the beginning of a systematic effort to remove them from public life and rob an entire generation of their future.
Today, girls have been banned from secondary schools and universities; women have been pushed out of workplaces; and restrictions on movement, expression, and participation in society have expanded. Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are prohibited from accessing secondary and higher education. More than 2 million adolescent girls have been denied their right to continue learning.
But five years later, the most troubling question is how the world learned to live with the Taliban’s policies toward women and girls.
Since August 2021, the language surrounding Afghanistan has changed. After the Taliban takeover, the world demanded the restoration of the rights of Afghan women and girls. Five years later, much of the conversation has shifted toward how to engage with the Taliban while raising concerns about women’s rights. The U.N. and other international community actors have adopted a policy of “principled engagement,” arguing that dialogue is needed to address Afghanistan’s humanitarian crisis while continuing to call for an end to restrictions on women and girls.
Engagement and diplomacy are complicated realities. Afghanistan is facing a humanitarian crisis, and millions of Afghans depend on international assistance. But there is a dangerous line between engaging with a country’s oppressive regime and allowing the systematic exclusion of half the population to become normalized. Consequently, the Taliban’s strategy has focused on waiting for global attention to its treatment of women to decline. Policies that once triggered international outrage have become just another item on the long list of Afghanistan’s unresolved crises.
The Taliban understood that controlling women’s lives requires controlling their visibility and silencing their voices. The restrictions began with education, but they expanded into broader efforts to remove women’s presence from public spaces, workplaces, media, and decision-making. According to the U.N., there have been more than 79 decrees and directives directly restricting the rights of Afghan women and girls since the Taliban takeover, while over 400 additional measures have indirectly affected nearly every aspect of their lives.
As a result, Afghan women’s voices have all but disappeared from public narratives. Afghanistan’s media landscape has faced enormous pressure since 2021. Female journalists have been pushed out, media organizations have operated under increasing restrictions, and public discussions about women’s rights have narrowed. UNESCO has noted that restrictions on women’s participation in media have tightened, including limitations preventing women from speaking on the radio.
This raises an uncomfortable question for Afghanistan’s media institutions: Are they documenting the reality Afghan women face, or are they, intentionally or not, contributing to its normalization?
Speaking at the Jaipur Literature Festival in London on June 6, Saad Mohseni, chairman and chief executive officer of MOBY Group, Afghanistan’s largest private media company, described conditions in Afghanistan as “normal,” stating that “women can walk around cities and drive without covering their faces.”
Yet while these remarks were being made in London, reports from Herat indicated that Taliban authorities were detaining dozens of women for allegedly violating the hijab rules – even though many were reportedly fully covered. The contrast between these accounts highlights the danger of describing life in Afghanistan as “normal” while women continue to face arbitrary enforcement of ever-changing restrictions.
Media organizations operate under extraordinary pressure in authoritarian environments, and survival often requires making difficult compromises. But journalism is about ensuring that the voices of those most affected are heard. When women disappear from newsrooms, interviews, and public conversations, their exclusion becomes easier to ignore – and easier to accept.

Across Afghanistan, women and girls have created alternative pathways to learning. They study via online platforms, home-based classrooms, and private initiatives. Teachers who once worked in schools have become educators in hidden classrooms. Students who lost access to formal education have searched for new ways to continue learning. Thus, technology has become more than a tool for Afghan girls, it has become a form of resistance.
These efforts demonstrate the courage and determination of Afghan women and girls who refuse to give up on education. They have created lifelines for learning when formal pathways have been taken away. But no alternative program can replace a functioning education system. A girl should not have to find a hidden classroom, secure a device, or overcome extraordinary barriers just to access a basic human right. Access to education for all should be guaranteed.
The consequences of excluding women from education will affect Afghanistan for generations. UNICEF has warned that continued restrictions on girls’ education will have devastating consequences for Afghanistan’s economy, healthcare system, and future workforce.
The Taliban may believe that limiting women’s education protects their vision of society. In reality, it is weakening the country. When a girl is denied education, she loses the chance to build her future; her family loses the hope of a daughter who could become a teacher, doctor, or leader; and Afghanistan loses the talent and potential of an entire generation of women.
The Taliban closed school doors, but Afghan women have continued searching for ways to open them.
In the last five years, the world has repeatedly praised Afghan women for their resilience. They have been called brave, determined, and inspirational. But their resilience should not provide an excuse for allowing this injustice to continue. 
The world has a responsibility to take concrete actions: to keep alternative pathways to learning open while formal education remains restricted; to provide sustained support to Afghan-led education initiatives; to hold the Taliban accountable for violating the fundamental right to education; and to ensure that women’s rights remain central in diplomatic engagement and continue working toward the day when every Afghan girl can return to a safe and recognized education system.

articles.title: Where Is Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi?
articles.full_text:
Sean Turnell, an economist and former advisor to the ousted leader, returns to Beyond The Mekong to discuss recent events in Myanmar.
A stencil graffiti image of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi by an unknown artist in Bangkok, Thailand.
The military-backed government in Myanmar this week released four photos of the country’s jailed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who met with Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative for the International Committee of the Red Cross in Myanmar, on August 3.
“This may be a first step, but it must not be the last,” her son, Kim Aris, said in a statement.
Sean Turnell, an Australian economist who worked with Suu Kyi and then shared a prison with her after the military coup in 2021, agrees, adding that “proof of life” is also required for some 20,000 people who are believed to be held as political prisoners inside Myanmar’s jails.
Turnell returned to Beyond the Mekong and spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about the first confirmation of Suu Kyi’s existence in many years and the issues facing the opposition National Unity Government (NUG) and the various armed groups battling the military.
The NUG, its People’s Defense Force (PDF), and the country’s numerous ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) have faced a resurgent military this year and a counter-offensive aimed at retaking territory won by the rebels during 2023 and 2024.
Min Aung Hlaing, the coup leader and now military-backed civilian leader, has also gone on a diplomatic offensive in search of international legitimacy for his administration within ASEAN, which wants the junta to return to its Five-Point Consensus as a roadmap for peace.
Turnell, who spent 650 days behind bars prior to his release in November 2022, says the civil war, which has claimed some 100,000 lives, cannot be won by the military, as the NUG and EAOs continue to formulate a federal framework for a country mired by ethnic differences. But eventually, he says, peace will prevail.

articles.title: Vietnam’s Top Leader To Lam to Pay State Visits to Australia and New Zealand
articles.full_text:
The visits are likely to build on the momentum created by the Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships signed recently with both countries.
To Lam, general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam and president of Vietnam, delivers a keynote address at the 23rd IISS Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, May 29, 2026.
Vietnam’s President To Lam will next week embark on state visits to Australia and New Zealand, the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday.
In a statement, it announced that Lam, who also serves as general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), would travel to the two nations from August 9 to 14, but did not specify the exact itinerary.
The trip, which has been rumored for several weeks, was confirmed by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s office, which said that Lam would be in Australia on August 9-12 and would meet with Albanese on August 11 in order “to discuss opportunities to deepen cooperation.”
“I look forward to welcoming General Secretary and President To Lam to Australia and discussing how we can strengthen cooperation between our two nations,” Albanese said in the statement. “The Vietnam-Australia relationship is grounded in deep strategic trust, mutual interests, and a shared ambition for the future of our region.”
The New Zealand government also confirmed that Lam would arrive in Auckland on August 12 and depart the following day.
The Vietnamese leader’s trip to Australia is likely to build on the momentum created by the two nations’ establishment of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in March 2024. This raised Australia to the highest tier of Vietnam’s diplomatic hierarchy, alongside Russia, China, and the United States, and pledged to develop “all aspects of our relationship,” including defense and security, trade, education, energy cooperation, and digital transformation.
Lam’s visit, his first to Australia since being appointed president in April, will “consolidate political trust at the highest level and provide fresh momentum for the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership,” Vietnam’s Ambassador to Australia Pham Hung Tam told state media.
It will also offer an opportunity for Lam and Albanese “to exchange views on regional and international issues of mutual concern and enhance coordination at multilateral forums, reaffirming their shared commitment to peace, stability, cooperation, and sustainable development,” Tam said.
According to a Reuters report, Vietnam and Australia “are expected to sign 12 to 16 agreements covering areas such as education, digital transformation, agriculture, and ​healthcare.”
Lam’s trip to New Zealand, the first by a Vietnamese president since 2007, also follows the establishment of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership last year, when Prime Minister ​Christopher Luxon described Vietnam as “incredibly important to New Zealand’s economic future.”
The move “reflects the high ambition and trust between our countries,” Luxon said in a statement yesterday. He added that Wellington and Hanoi ​aimed to ⁠strengthen ties “across food and fiber, education, tourism, technology, aviation and investment, supporting more exports and jobs here ⁠at ​home.”
In New Zealand, officials anticipate ⁠the signing of five or six agreements with their Vietnamese counterparts, Reuters reported.
In addition to the obvious economic complementarities, Vietnam’s relationships with Australia and New Zealand have been fortified by a shared concern about China’s growing maritime clout and ambition – an issue that was referenced in the joint statements announcing the establishment of both Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships. However, Hanoi continues to place great value in its relationship with Beijing, and in part due to the increasingly unpredictable and capricious nature of U.S. foreign policymaking under President Donald Trump, has doubled down on its omnivorous foreign policy approach, which seeks to create good relationships with countries on both sides of the global strategic divide.
This is reflected in Lam’s busy travel schedule since his appointment as CPV general secretary in August 2024. Over the past two years, he has paid official visits to China, Russia, Belarus, and Cuba, as well as the U.S., France, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, and regional partners like Indonesia, Singapore, and Malaysia.
Most significantly, he has spearheaded the creation of Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships with France (October 2024), Malaysia (November 2024), New Zealand (February 2025), Indonesia (March 2025), Singapore (March 2025), Thailand (May 2025), the U.K. (October 2025), and the European Union (January 2026). Since his appointment as president in April, Lam has also paid official visits to China, India, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Singapore, and the Philippines.

articles.title: Japan’s Billions Are the Wildcard in Southeast Asia’s Aid Race
articles.full_text:
Few development actors in the region can currently match Tokyo’s combination of credibility and quality.
For the last two decades, the contest for influence in Southeast Asia has almost always been conceptualized as a two-horse race: China floods the region with infrastructure loans and the United States counters with democracy programs and health assistance. This binary framing obscures the presence of a third player, one whose role may prove more decisive than either Washington or Beijing: Japan.
For decades, Tokyo has without fanfare underwritten much of Southeast Asia’s development. According to the Lowy Institute’s 2025 Southeast Asia Aid Map, Japan disbursed around $35 billion in development finance to the region between 2015 and 2023. This is less than China’s $50 billion in actual disbursements, but far more than the United States’ $9 billion. More critically, Japan’s assistance arrives as grants and concessional loans governed by transparent standards, governance principles, and environmental safeguards. In official development finance share for 2022, Japan (30 percent) and the Western bloc combined (31 percent) still outpaced China (24 percent) across Southeast Asia, a fact routinely drowned out by headlines announcing each new Belt and Road mega-project.
Japan’s dominance in the region’s development landscape is not new. For much of the post-war era, Tokyo has treated its overseas development assistance (ODA) as a strategic instrument linking infrastructure to trade expansion and the cultivation of stable bilateral ties. The Fukuda Doctrine of 1977 institutionalized this commitment, resulting in decades of accumulated trust.
That trust is now being tested. Since 2013, China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has dramatically reshuffled regional development finance. Beijing has committed approximately $149 billion to Southeast Asia, concentrating flows overwhelmingly in transport and energy infrastructure. The competition came into sharpest relief during the bidding war for Indonesia’s Jakarta-Bandung high-speed railway, a contest Japan ultimately lost to China. China’s financing proposal was distinguished by shorter projected delivery timelines and a comparatively limited set of conditionalities, while Japan’s competing offer emphasized more stringent technical benchmarks and governance requirements as preconditions for engagement. Indonesia’s selection of China’s bid reflected a preference for speed and cost over structural prudence. 
The subsequent trajectory of the project, which was marked by protracted delays, significant cost overruns, and contentious contractual renegotiations, provides an instructive case study of the governance risks associated with infrastructure financing arrangements. It demonstrates, in particular, the financial vulnerabilities that can emerge when recipient governments prioritize short-term fiscal attractiveness over rigorous due diligence and careful assessment of life-cycle costs.
This episode reflects a structural limitation in China’s development model. Approximately 71 percent of China’s official development finance in Southeast Asia consists of non-concessional, commercially-oriented lending rather than genuine aid. Beijing’s infrastructure support functions more like club goods, which benefit specific bilateral partners and Chinese state-owned contractors, rather than universal public goods. Health, education, and governance each receive less than 1 percent of China’s regional disbursements. These are precisely the domains in which the United States has historically focused its aid efforts in the region.

In any event, there’s more to the picture than Japan substituting for diminished U.S. engagement or serving as a direct counterweight to Chinese influence. Rather, Tokyo’s sustained presence as a standards-based development financier expands recipient governments’ bargaining space vis-à-vis Beijing. This has important geopolitical implications. As the cases of Vietnam and Indonesia illustrate, Southeast Asian governments have demonstrated considerable sophistication in leveraging competing donor offers to extract more favorable financing conditions. Governments of ASEAN countries should recognize this, and Japan, for its part, should say so more loudly and with considerably greater ambition.

articles.title: Was Tarique Rahman’s Youth Outreach More Than an Election Strategy?
articles.full_text:
The BNP’s credibility with Bangladesh’s youth will ultimately depend not on whether the government can deliver jobs, fair recruitment, and meaningful participation in state-building.
Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman meets with youth at Bangladesh Army Stadium in Dhaka, July 27, 2026.
After 17 years in exile, Tarique Rahman, then acting chairman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), returned to Dhaka on December 25, 2025. By then, people’s political aspirations had changed significantly through a mass uprising and political transition following a long period of authoritarian rule. 
In the aftermath of the July 2024 uprising, Bangladesh’s youth had moved to the center of politics. They not only led the movement that brought down Sheikh Hasina’s government, but also made up a significant portion of the electorate that would choose the next. The youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP) emerged in the political arena; most of its leaders had been at the forefront of the July uprising. Ahead of the national election, Jamaat-e-Islami, in alliance with the NCP and several other Islamist parties, was mounting a political challenge.
Rahman and his party did not take long to recognize the reality. After returning home, he placed young people at the center of various programs, policy plans, and the party’s election manifesto. During the election campaign, several events were organized exclusively for the youth. At that time, analysts viewed them as part of the BNP’s strategy to attract young voters.
The formal campaign for Bangladesh’s 13th parliamentary election began on January 22 this year. On that day, Rahman was in Sylhet, a city around 250 kilometers from Dhaka. He attended an event titled “The Plan: Youth Policy Talk with Tarique Rahman,” where several hundred students from different educational institutions heard the leader of the country’s largest political party explain his plans for nation-building. The students also shared their views and raised questions. Rahman responded to them and sought their suggestions. A similar event was later held in Chattogram. He also engaged directly with the youth through other programs.
The BNP’s election manifesto contained many promises for the youth. The party pledged to create 10 million new jobs within five years by attracting domestic and foreign investment. The government is now making efforts to bring in such investment. During recent visits to Malaysia and China, Rahman – now the prime minister – met executives of leading business organizations, and the government has repeatedly said that Bangladesh is open for investment. 
Law and order has improved since the BNP government took office on February 17, and the political environment has become relatively stable. However, the employment pledge faces structural constraints. Bangladesh’s unreliable energy supply has prevented hundreds of industrial units from beginning production, even after completing other preparations. Unless the government can improve energy security and infrastructure, investment-driven job creation will remain difficult.
Other BNP commitments included sending 10 million workers abroad, introducing unemployment benefits, involving young people in national development and state-building, providing freelancing and outsourcing training at higher education institutions, and offering small office spaces to young entrepreneurs in IT parks. It will take time to determine how many of these commitments are ultimately implemented.
As the government approaches the completion of its first six months in office, a question is being raised: were these election-time promises and the BNP leadership’s attempts to connect with the youth merely strategies to secure their votes? The question is not unreasonable, particularly after Gen Z students sitting for the Higher Secondary Certificate examinations recently blocked roads in Dhaka and elsewhere in the country for  a few days. There may be questions about the extent to which young people are being given opportunities to participate in state-building. 
Nevertheless, the BNP’s top leader has remained engaged with the youth since coming to power. Before taking office, Rahman prioritized dialogue over the traditional format of one-way speeches at rallies and public events. Continuing that approach may have become more difficult after assuming the office of prime minister. Even so, he has occasionally invited content creators, athletes, and entrepreneurs to his office to hear about their challenges and concerns. There have been around a dozen such examples since February 17.
The BNP government launched Notun Kuri Sports, a nationwide program to identify talented children and adolescents; transformed the parliament complex into an open civic education platform for students; and allocated 5 billion taka for a startup fund. 
A review of the government’s activities suggests that it is placing emphasis on protecting the future through climate action and developing the younger generation. Programs are under way to plant 250 million trees and excavate canals over five years. At the same time, the government is prioritizing technical education and introducing compulsory foreign-language learning.
Yet the BNP’s credibility with Bangladesh’s youth will ultimately depend not on meetings and programs, but on whether the government can deliver jobs, fair recruitment, and meaningful participation in state-building.
Bangladesh had a total of 127,711,793 registered voters in the last election. Under the country’s National Youth Policy, citizens between the ages of 18 and 35 are defined as youth. According to Election Commission data, nearly 50 million voters fell within this age group. That means more than one-third of the electorate was young. It is clear that they played a decisive role in the BNP’s electoral victory. As expected, they now want the government to fulfil promises such as employment opportunities.
Whether they are described as Gen Z or simply as the youth, they want access to education and employment. Recruitment and investment decisions must also be protected from political interference. After all, the July 2024 mass uprising began with intense student dissatisfaction over the quota system for entry into government service, even if the wider context for the uprising was created by the Awami League government’s decade and a half of authoritarian rule. 
Tarique Rahman and his party’s youth engagement before and after the election sought to introduce a new approach to politics. Clearly, they understood the demands of the time. But it is still too early to determine whether those promises will ultimately be implemented.

articles.title: How South Korea Can Survive the Unbundling of International Order
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s strategic challenges – and the potential solutions – make the case for democratic multilateralism.
For most of the post-war era, power, legitimacy, and cooperation reinforced one another. American leadership underwrote security, open markets, and freedom of navigation. Democratic partnerships generated political trust. Universal institutions such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, and the nuclear nonproliferation regime provided common rules and legal legitimacy. Though imperfect, these three pillars generally worked in concert.
That alignment has broken down. Security, economic governance, political legitimacy, and practical cooperation are no longer occurring in the same institutions or even among the same groups of states. I call this structural transformation the “unbundling of order.” The result is disalignment, a condition in which power, legitimacy, and cooperation no longer reinforce one another.
Analysts today often ask whether the liberal international order is collapsing or which great power will replace the United States. The real question is whether the essential functions of the international order can be reconnected under increasingly fragmented geopolitical conditions. 
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exposed the inability of existing institutions like the United Nations to prevent or halt great power aggression. The ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran demonstrated that military superiority alone cannot ensure regional stability or the credibility of the global nonproliferation regime. Competition – especially, but not exclusively between China and the United States – over semiconductors, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, and maritime supply chains blurs the traditional boundary between economics and security. 
Cooperation is increasingly necessary, but the most inclusive institutions are often the least capable of collective action. This paradox has driven the rise of minilateralism. Smaller groups of like-minded partners can coordinate quickly, protect sensitive technologies, strengthen supply chain resilience, and respond effectively to shared threats. But while minilateral coalitions can act quickly, they lack broad legitimacy. Meanwhile, universal institutions provide legal authority and political inclusion but often struggle to act. 
Neither is sufficient alone. Democratic multilateralism must combine legitimacy with operational capacity. 
This is why democracy itself retains strategic importance. Democratic multilateralism is more than cooperation among states with shared political values. It provides a foundation for institutional trust. Intelligence sharing, advanced technology cooperation, defense industrial integration, financial coordination, and resilient supply chains all depend on confidence that partners will safeguard sensitive information, uphold long-term commitments, and remain accountable despite changes in government. Democratic governments may disagree, yet transparent institutions and political accountability make sustained strategic cooperation more credible. 
South Korea stands at the intersection of today’s defining strategic challenges: nuclear deterrence, China-U.S. competition, technological rivalry, supply chain resilience, and democratic cooperation. Its security depends on the alliance with the United States, its prosperity on an open global economy, and its future competitiveness on reliable technology networks. Few countries are therefore more exposed to the unbundling of order or better positioned to shape what follows.
Seoul must continue to diversify its partnerships, but diversification alone is not a strategy. It needs an organizing logic that connects its alliances, partnerships, markets, and institutions. It must determine which functions remain anchored in the U.S. alliance, which require broader networks, and how smaller, function-specific coalitions can be linked to or nested within broader regional and global institutions. 
For South Korea, deterrence will continue to depend primarily on the U.S. alliance. Technological resilience requires secure networks for protecting sensitive knowledge and coordinating investment. Economic security depends on diversified markets, suppliers, and production chains. Wider institutions remain essential for common rules, political inclusion, and international acceptance. The task is to make these different frameworks, each built for different purposes, mutually reinforcing. 
South Korea should therefore seek not simply to balance among great powers, but to develop connective power: the capacity to align security commitments, economic partnerships, technological networks, and multilateral institutions around compatible purposes. This is a distinctive source of middle power influence. It rests not only on institutional access, but on a reputation for reliability, effective brokerage, and contributions to regional and global public goods. States with that standing can bridge alliances, functional coalitions, and wider institutions, and thereby shape the terms of cooperation. 
The post-war order cannot simply be restored because the architecture that sustained it has already changed. But that doesn’t mean the world is doomed to a fate of closed and competing blocs. Instead, the more plausible alternative is not a singular order but several layered and overlapping ones. States will pursue national interests through different arrangements while cooperating where regional stability and global public goods require collective action. The most indispensable states will not necessarily dominate every arena, but will make cooperation across arenas possible.
For South Korea, bridging these system is a national imperative. Its security, prosperity, technological competitiveness, and diplomatic autonomy depend on its ability to operate across multiple institutional systems. 
This essay is one of four to emerge from discussions at an international conference jointly organized by the Seoul Forum for International Affairs and the Hairan Series of Korea University’s Institute for Interdisciplinary Unification Studies, “Democratic Multilateralism at the Edge,” held in Seoul on April 20, 2026.

articles.title: The Rule of Law in Afghanistan Failed Long Before the Taliban’s Triumph
articles.full_text:
To be rightfully concerned about the present is not an excuse to distort the past.
Nearly five years after Taliban insurgents toppled the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, calls still ring out for a return to the rule of law. United Nations officials contend that Taliban governance “precipitated the collapse of the rule of law and judicial independence in Afghanistan.” Amnesty International pleads for the Taliban to “reinstate a formal constitutional and legal framework and the rule of law.”
The idea that Afghanistan lost the rule of law in 2021 is compelling. It is also a fantasy. The United States, and the international community more broadly, abandoned rule of law in Afghanistan long before the Taliban returned. 
The U.S.-backed regime that the Taliban defeated was one of the most corrupt states on Earth. And within that regime, police and courts were consistently ranked among the most corrupt parts. For example, a major 2018 survey found “corruption within the local security and justice sector in Afghanistan remains a key driver of insecurity in the country.” The United States’ willingness to not only tolerate but also perpetuate corruption and lawlessness proved essential for the Taliban’s success.
What of the U.S. role? Here, too, reality and rhetoric clash. Government officials and outside commentators routinely stress the idea that progress in law and justice was occurring and would have continued. As my recent work in Law & Social Inquiry shows, this is not the case.
At first, the U.S. envisioned the new Islamic Republic of Afghanistan as committed to the rule of law. Yet, initial efforts were outsourced to Italy and achieved little. Worse still, they backed a strong presidency and an unrepresentative parliamentary system that offered a decidedly weak foundation for a state built on the rule of law. 
As the Taliban insurgency gathered strength in the mid 2000s, Afghan government corruption became a key concern. Courts were expensive, unprofessional, predatory, and generally ineffective. While ordinary people suffered, impunity became the norm for the powerful. This prompted U.S. President George W. Bush to pledge to “replace the rule of the Taliban with the rule of law.” 
Initial U.S. efforts focused on legislative reform, capacity building, and increased public engagement. Yet, they failed to stem the Taliban insurgency or improve justice. Aid programs focused on improving knowledge and reforming laws, but bad laws and insufficient knowledge were not the real problems. Those were law and governance rooted in injustice.
U.S. President Barack Obama promised to fix the deteriorating situation in Afghanistan. The so-called Afghan Surge (2010–2014) sought to improve law and order and support lasting military gains. The surge poured in vast resources but on a short timeline to defeat the Taliban and establish a stable, democratic Afghanistan. In doing so, Obama went beyond Bush in trying to work directly with powerful tribal authorities, who had long maintained order throughout much of the country. To counter lingering security challenges, the military itself became directly involved in rule of law aid.
The practical results, however, were profoundly disappointing. Resources mattered little absent a commitment to rule of law ideals. Non-state justice actors were hesitant to cast their lot with the internationally backed regime. Military units faced the same chronic problems of insecurity and inability to transform rule of law programing into rule of law realities. 
After 2014, however, a subtle but profound change happened. The U.S. still officially backed the rule of law, but innovation ceased. Instead of trying to innovate or push the Afghan government toward real reforms, the U.S. continued to back the same policies and programs that had already failed. For instance, Surge-era USAID program implementers explicitly noted the pervasive corruption alongside “weak political support for rule of law reforms,” and “a lack of willingness…to support and adopt reforms.” Nevertheless, the next round of rule of law programing set a goal of “combating corruption by empowering relevant Afghan Government agencies/institutions.”
For the rest of Obama’s second term and all of President Donald Trump’s first term, rule of law efforts were symbolic. U.S. policymakers were keen to signal they had not abandoned the rule of law in Afghanistan. However, they no longer sought to change realities on the ground. Previously unsuccessful strategies and programing were uncritically replicated. So too were partnerships with disinterested, uncooperative Afghan stakeholders. 
No consideration was given to why earlier efforts failed, and frequently, there were even denials that they had failed. Official rule of law policy embraced highly optimistic or even outright false assumptions and lacked credibility as policy or practice. Not only did U.S. rule of law efforts fail from 2015 onward, but there was no plausible vision for how they could have succeeded. 
Failing programs are unlikely to start working somehow. Nor are corrupt institutions and actors going to stop being corrupt simply by providing additional resources or training. Even the flagship U.S.-funded anti-corruption initiative itself was exposed as deeply corrupt. Failing efforts were consistently tolerated because the political consequences of admitting failure were deemed higher than the practical consequences of supporting failing policy.
What can be learned from this failure? First and foremost, policymakers ignore justice at their peril. After all, profound law and justice failures provided the initial opening for a renewed insurgency. Effective legal order constituted the core of the Taliban’s political program, it underpinned their claim to be Afghanistan’s legitimate rulers, and it highlighted the previous state justice system’s failures. Taliban justice, while undeniably brutal, sought to provide what state courts could not: locally intelligible and legitimate justice. 
U.S. policymakers were so fearful that the Taliban might return to power that they were not prepared to meaningfully challenge the regime’s increasingly anti-democratic tendencies. U.S. officials did not attempt to prevent another hopelessly compromised presidential election in 2019. After a prolonged deadlock, U.S. diplomats brokered another National Unity Government. Despite the instability and loss of legitimacy triggered by earlier electoral crises, U.S. policymakers gave up on trying to ensure anything resembling a fair vote. Disinterest in democracy, as with the rule of law, made an already tenuous regime ever more brittle. 
Logically, for the Afghan government to be a credible partner for peace, or even simply to endure, it required real legitimacy. The U.S.-backed government needed to offer credible law and order held in at least roughly the same esteem as Taliban justice. Beyond that, it needed to stand for values that large swathes of the Afghan population were willing to fight to preserve. The regime collapsed before U.S. troops even completed their withdrawal. Ultimately, pursuing symbolic rule of law promotion had very real and disastrous consequences. It also shows that international actors must make law and justice a real priority, not just a rhetorical one.
The end result has been more suffering for ordinary Afghans under an increasingly harsh Taliban rule and ongoing humanitarian disaster. These concerns very much deserve attention. To be rightfully concerned about the present, however, is not an excuse to distort the past.
Nearly five years after Taliban insurgents toppled the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, calls still ring out for a return to the rule of law. United Nations officials contend that Taliban governance “precipitated the collapse of the rule of law and judicial independence in Afghanistan.” Amnesty International pleads for the Taliban to “reinstate a formal constitutional and legal framework and the rule of law.”
The idea that Afghanistan lost the rule of law in 2021 is compelling. It is also a fantasy. The United States, and the international community more broadly, abandoned rule of law in Afghanistan long before the Taliban returned. 
The U.S.-backed regime that the Taliban defeated was one of the most corrupt states on Earth. And within that regime, police and courts were consistently ranked among the most corrupt parts. What of the U.S. role? Here, too, reality and rhetoric clash. Government officials and outside commentators routinely stress the idea that progress in law and justice was occurring and would have continued. As my recent work in Law & Social Inquiry shows, this is not the case.

Initial U.S. efforts focused on legislative reform, capacity building, and increased public engagement. Yet, they failed to stem the Taliban insurgency or improve justice. articles.title: Bangladesh-India Relations Hit Fresh Turbulence
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh expressed “outrage” even as India said it had nothing to do with Sheikh Hasina’s online media engagement at the Awami League presser in New Delhi.
File photo of Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, May 2, 2024.
Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has said she will return to her country in December this year, almost two and a half years after fleeing to India following violent student protests that culminated in the ouster of her government.
In a message delivered online to Indian and foreign journalists in New Delhi on August 5, Hasina said her decision to return home was based on her desire to serve her country and its people. Acknowledging the possibility of imprisonment or even execution if she returned to Bangladesh, Hasina said that such apprehensions would not deter her.
“My return, and the return of the Awami League to the democratic process, is not about power. It is about putting Bangladesh back on the right track,” Hasina said. She also defended her government’s action against protesters who she said had destroyed public infrastructure and vandalized monuments associated with Sheikh Mujibur Rehman, who led Bangladesh’s liberation war in 1971 and became independent Bangladesh’s first president.
Hasina’s media interaction drew an angry response from the Bangladesh Nationalist Party government, which expressed “outrage” over India allowing the press conference to be organized in Delhi. “Dhaka deeply regrets that in spite of concerns conveyed a priori to the Government of India about the likely ramifications of this event on the reset of our bilateral relations, this public event was permitted to be held,” it said. That it took place on the very day that Bangladesh was observing the second anniversary of Hasina’s ouster was “an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh and a grievous insult to the martyrs of the July Revolution,” it added.
On the eve of Hasina’s online interaction with the media, India distanced itself from the Hasina event, saying it had no role in it nor had it endorsed it. The Awami League presser was hosted by the Foreign Correspondents Club of South Asia in New Delhi.
Hasina had deployed extreme force to quell the protests of summer 2024, which led to over a thousand people getting killed in the crackdown. She was forced to step down on August 5, 2024.
She fled to India after the fall of her government. India’s sheltering of Hasina since then has irked Bangladeshis immensely, especially after November 2025, when a special Bangladeshi tribunal convicted and sentenced Hasina and her Home Minister Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal to death for crimes against humanity. Besides, Hasina had issued statements and given media interviews while in India, prompting Dhaka to repeatedly ask India to curb her political activities on Indian soil. Dhaka has also sought her extradition to face justice in Bangladesh. However, India has ignored Dhaka’s requests.
Forcing Hasina back to Bangladesh is not an option for India. Her return of her own volition may help ease the current tensions in Bangladesh-India ties.

When Hasina was in power, the Bangladesh-India relationship was warm. That changed with her ouster, especially when the interim government under Mohammed Yunus leaned toward China and seemed insensitive to Indian concerns.

Foreign Minister Khalilur Rehman’s visit to New Delhi in April was seen as a confidence-rebuilding exercise. Yet India remains wary, largely because of the BNP government’s growing closeness to Pakistan, China, and Turkiye.
For India, stable ties with Bangladesh are a priority given that the two share a 4,100-km-long border. India looks for support from Dhaka not only for greater connectivity with its landlocked Northeast but also to deal with insurgencies in this restive region.

The envoy, Dinesh Trivedi, was also elevated to cabinet minister status to ease his access to the Bangladeshi prime minister.
India has also invited Rahman to the BRICS summit in Delhi in September, although the Bangladeshi prime minister is yet to accept the invite.
An important issue that could shape bilateral relations decisively is the Ganga Water Sharing Accord. Signed in 1996 when Hasina first became prime minister, the treaty is valid for 30 years. It is up for renewal this December. A quick renewal could help place New Delhi’s ties with Dhaka on a firmer footing.

Previously, Mamata Banerjee, chief minister of West Bengal, had opposed a pact.

articles.title: Clashes Erupt at Susta Along India-Nepal Border
articles.full_text:
India and Nepal have settled almost 98 percent of their border. Differences over Kalapani and Susta have proven difficult to resolve.
The long-standing India-Nepal dispute over Susta, one of the most geographically and politically sensitive sections of the Nepal-India border, erupted in violent clashes on August 2 between Nepali villagers and Indian border security personnel.
The latter had allegedly crossed into Nepali territory in Nawalparasi West and dismantled an under-construction embankment built by local residents to prevent flooding. Nepal’s Armed Police Force had to intervene to prevent further escalation.
According to Nepali media, a similar iincident happened in June, when India’s Border Security Force personnel entered an embankment construction site in Susta Municipality-5 and pressured workers to halt the project, which was part of ongoing efforts to provide protection for flood-prone settlements in the area. India is yet to respond officially to these allegations.
India and Nepal share a 1,800-km-long open border. Susta in southern Nepal and the Kalapani-Limpiyadhura-Lipulekh area to Nepal’s west are disputed.
With regard to the dispute over Susta, there are no boundary pillars along the 24-km stretch of this region, and India and Nepal rely on natural features such as rivers and trees to mark the boundary. The shifting course of the Gandak (also known as Narayani) river, the midstream of which formed the boundary under the Treaty of Sugauli of 1816, has further complicated the border problem here.
Citing official sources from Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Nepali media publication reported that the Nepali Embassy in New Delhi raised Sunday’s clashes at Susta with India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) immediately. India’s position, according to this source, was that since the area where the embankment was built is disputed, the construction violates the “status quo” maintained between the two countries. India’s MEA is yet to issue a comment on this incident.
Nepali parliamentarians, who raised the issue in the House of Representatives, denounced the Indian security forces’ alleged actions and demanded the Indian government conduct an investigation into the incident and engage in diplomatic dialogue to “immediately stop the encroachment and threats.”
Such incidents are not uncommon; unresolved boundary disputes and competing territorial claims do periodically create tensions.
The India-Nepal border issue has erupted to the fore from time to time. In 2020, Nepal’s parliament passed a constitutional amendment to include a new political map that depicted the disputed Kalapani-Limpiyadhura-Lipulekh region as part of Nepal’s sovereign territory, which India rejected. Previously, Nepal had objected to New Delhi showing these territories as part of the Indian state of Uttarakhand.
On May 3 this year, Nepal objected to India and China’s plan to conduct the 2026 Kailash Mansarovar Yatra and restart border trade via the Lipulekh Pass as it traverses the disputed territory. New Delhi dismissed these claims as “unjustified,” describing Kathmandu’s “unilateral artificial enlargement” of territorial claims as “untenable.” Despite Kathmandu’s objection, India and China have resumed bilateral trade through the pass.
While India and Nepal have settled almost 98 percent of their border, disputes over Susta and Kalapani have proven difficult to resolve.
Back in 2014, both sides agreed that the border issue would be resolved through the mechanism involving the Boundary Working Group (BWG) and foreign secretaries. While the BWG, deals with boundary issues, such as construction, restoration and repair of boundary pillars and other technical tasks, the dispute over demarcation of territory in Susta and Kalapani is dealt with at the foreign secretary level.
Notably, while the BWG has met several times — most recently in July 2025 — no dedicated meeting at the foreign secretary level as part of the boundary resolution mechanism has taken place in the past 12 years.
In August 2025, Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri visited Nepal. However, the focus of the visit was on development cooperation. There was no mention of discussions on the border dispute in press statements released after Misri’s visit.
Similarly, following Nepali Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal’s visit to India in June this year, statements issued by the Nepal embassy in Delhi and India’s MEA made no reference to discussions on the boundary dispute or any border-related issues.
Nevertheless, beyond being a permanent political irritant in bilateral ties, the boundary dispute has not significantly derailed ties. Successful operational coordination between Indian security forces and their Nepali counterparts and strong bilateral ties across multiple domains spanning trade, development cooperation, civilizational links, etc., have largely averted border disputes from escalating into major diplomatic crises.
In fact, the exceptionally open nature of the border with minimal fencing on both sides — unlike India’s heavily militarized borders with Pakistan and China — is widely regarded as symbolic of the special relationship shared by the two countries.
The current status quo on the border privileges India, which has a strong security presence of security personnel to protect its borders.
However, the damage caused by the repeated flare-ups of the border dispute — which has even resulted in deaths on the Nepali side — percolates to the grassroots level, aggravating strong anti-India sentiments in Nepal. This bodes negatively for India’s influence in South Asia at large, which rests heavily on its close civilizational and people-to-people links with its smaller neighbors. More dangerously, it opens space for third countries such as China to exploit and build their political clout to challenge Indian dominance in the region.
The border dispute is unlikely to snowball into a geopolitical regional flashpoint due to the asymmetrical relationship between the two countries, given Nepal’s strong economic dependence on India and much smaller size. However, if New Delhi continues to stall and brush Kathmandu’s concerns under the rug, it is likely to cause damage to its interests and influence in the region, especially at a time when relations with other neighbors are in peril.
Political trust and diplomatic dialogue are the way forward. What is missing is a sense of urgency to resolve the dispute, especially from New Delhi. Nepal Prime Minister Balen Shah’s upcoming visit to India provides New Delhi with an opportunity to address long-standing issues and redefine its relationship with one of its closest neighbors.

articles.title: China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Law is Already Harming Uyghurs
articles.full_text:
Government actions that could once be described as regional campaigns are now embedded in national legislation. Restrictions will become easier to expand and harder to challenge.
China’s new Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress has been in effect for more than one month. Beijing claims the law will foster cohesion and protect the rights of minorities. In reality, it is already doing the opposite. One month in, the law is already harming Uyghurs and other ethnic groups and dissidents. Governments must take decisive action to challenge the law and protect diaspora communities before it is too late.
As numerous sources have warned, the new law codifies a dramatic shift away from even the promise of regional autonomy, instead embedding Xi Jinping’s campaign of forced assimilation into nearly every facet of government and public life. In doing so, the law violates China’s own constitution. 
For Uyghurs, this is not new. In 2017, a Chinese official summarized the government’s strategy toward Uyghurs: “Break their lineage, break their roots, break their connections, and break their origins.” 
Since then, Chinese authorities have systematically dismantled Uyghur social, cultural, and religious life in what the United States government and numerous national parliaments have formally recognized as genocide and crimes against humanity. The indoctrination Uyghurs faced in internment camps, where authorities sought to replace Islam and Uyghur identity with loyalty to the CCP, is now imposed in daily life across the Uyghur homeland of East Turkestan.
What has changed is this: Government actions that could once be described as regional campaigns are now embedded in national legislation. These restrictions will become easier to expand and harder to challenge.
The new law makes schools, religious institutions, all levels of government, and even families responsible for instilling and enforcing the CCP’s definition of “ethnic unity.” It requires parents to “educate and guide minors to love the Chinese Communist Party,” replaces bilingual education with Mandarin beginning in preschool, and requires religious institutions to persist in the “Sinicization” of religion. In other words, all children must be raised to love the CCP, all languages must give way to Mandarin, and any faith is permitted only when reshaped to serve the state.
The law’s effects are already visible. Videos on Chinese social media show Uyghur-language signs being removed from city streets and replaced with Chinese. Uyghurs are unable to resist, or even express sadness, as CCP cadres watch. Any negative reaction can be labeled resistance to “ethnic unity,” placing a person at risk of interrogation, detention, and arrest.
Just three days after the law took effect, two Uyghur sisters and their mother were reportedly arrested for sending merchandise to another sister in Turkiye. They were accused of “supporting terrorism” for helping with her business. While it is not new for authorities to penalize Uyghurs for contacting family abroad, the ethnic unity law gives an already abusive system an even broader vocabulary with which to characterize normal family ties, cultural expression, and overseas contact as threats to national unity.
The danger also extends to individuals beyond China’s borders. As many have warned, Article 63 of the law declares that organizations and individuals overseas can be pursued for activities Beijing claims undermine ethnic unity or create ethnic division. Chinese officials have openly defended the government’s claimed authority to target people abroad under this provision, creating yet another pretext for transnational repression against Uyghurs, Tibetans, Southern Mongolians, and other diaspora groups or dissidents. 
This too is already taking effect. In Kazakhstan, Uyghurs and others with ties to East Turkestan report “feeling the pressure” since the law’s enactment. Dolkun Isa – a prominent Uyghur activist, former president of the World Uyghur Congress, and German citizen – was recently detained and deported from Morocco while traveling to attend a religious freedom conference. Such cases demonstrate how China uses its influence to pressure other governments to restrict or intimidate Uyghurs on its behalf.
The claim that overseas individuals may face legal responsibility for “undermining ethnic unity” should alarm every government. Uyghurs, Tibetans, Hong Kongers, Falun Gong practitioners, Chinese dissidents, and Taiwanese advocates should not have to wonder whether exercising their freedoms abroad will place themselves or their relatives in danger.
The international response has been inadequate thus far, limited to statements rather than actionable commitments. U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk called for the law’s repeal. Eight U.N. special rapporteurs for human rights expressed serious concern. The European Parliament urged China to repeal the law, and the European Union and Taiwan warned about its extraterritorial reach. Australian officials reportedly raised concerns with their Chinese counterparts. 
The United States in particular has been noticeably quiet, as the Trump administration has yet to take a public stance. A State Department spokesperson called the measure “problematic,” and members of Congress urged a stronger response, but informal remarks and congressional statements are not enough. Governments, including the United States, should issue clear public condemnations, demand the law’s repeal, and make clear that China has no jurisdiction over lawful speech in other countries. Furthermore, governments should coordinate to protect diaspora communities from the transnational repression the law enables. To do so here in the U.S., Congress should pass the Uyghur Policy Act of 2025 and Transnational Repression Policy Act. 
The damage caused by China’s ethnic unity law is no longer hypothetical. Governments must respond with urgency before forced assimilation and transnational repression become even more deeply entrenched.
